title: Chapter XX
summary: A midnight cry leads Jane into Thornfield's hidden violence. Rochester orders her to tend the bleeding Mason in silence beside a locked inner room while he fetches a surgeon; Mason later says a woman bit and stabbed him. Rochester removes Mason before dawn and continues blaming Grace Poole. In the orchard he presents Jane with a hypothetical version of his own grave past error and asks whether love may justify crossing a conventional barrier. Jane answers that repentance cannot depend on another human being and defines her loyalty as obedience only in what is right.
events: Mason is attacked in the third-storey chamber, and Rochester suppresses alarm among his guests.
Jane silently tends Mason while a dangerous woman remains locked in the adjoining room.
A surgeon treats wounds made by a knife and teeth, and Mason is secretly sent away before sunrise.
Rochester tests Jane with a moral parable about an old error, a new beloved, and an obstacle he calls merely conventional.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.development: Proves brave and dependable but explicitly limits devotion by conscience: she will help Rochester only in what she believes right.

characters.name: Edward Rochester
characters.development: Appears as both protector and deceiver, desperate to preserve a secret that obstructs the happiness he seeks through Jane.

characters.name: Richard Mason
characters.development: Becomes the wounded witness to the imprisoned woman's violence yet submits to Rochester's demand for secrecy.

themes: conscience as a limit on love

threads.text: The concealed woman is violent, is known to Mason, and is managed by Rochester and Grace Poole.
Rochester's past 'error' creates a continuing obstacle to union with the person he sees as regenerative.
Jane's stated refusal to do wrong foreshadows a direct conflict between love and conscience.
